what_it_does: FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays — chips whose internal circuitry can be reprogrammed after manufacture) are increasingly used in cloud servers, and multiple tenants may share one chip. A known risk is that malicious logic placed on the chip can spy on other tenants' computations by measuring tiny fluctuations in power draw — a 'power side-channel attack.' Prior work assumed the attacker needed to place special sensing circuits on the same chip and share a power rail with the victim. AmpereBleed shows that this assumption is too conservative: many ARM-FPGA system-on-chip boards (devices that combine a conventional CPU with an FPGA on one package) already include small current-monitoring chips called INA226 sensors, intended for ordinary power management. This paper demonstrates that reading those off-the-shelf sensors is enough to detect and exploit power signatures — identifying what workload a victim is running and potentially extracting secret information — without any custom circuitry planted by the attacker.
